findings.message: Quoted material attributed to EurekAlert! does not match the source verbatim.
findings.details: Article quotes: "made famous in the 1980s by physicist Richard Feynman's failed experimental attempts to resolve it." The EurekAlert!/NYU press release actually reads: "made famous in the 1980s by physicist Richard Feynman's account of his failed experiments." The underlying fact (Feynman made the problem famous in the 1980s) is accurate, but the wording inside quote marks is a paraphrase, not a verbatim quote.

## Overview

A team led by mathematicians at New York University has produced what they describe as the experimental answer to Feynman's Sprinkler Problem, a fluid-dynamics puzzle that asks how a sprinkler behaves when water is drawn into it rather than sprayed out. editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece (848 words, within the 400-1200 range) following the Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know / Analysis format. Clear, neutral summary of a niche physics/fluid-dynamics study with appropriate technical depth and honest acknowledgment of unreported figures (exact torque values, jet-collision angle) in the 'What We Don't Know' section.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 4 sources personally verified. source-0.html.gz (NYU, 200, sha256 ca1ef98e...) read in full — confirms the momentum-flux finding, the Mach and Feynman rival theories and why each was ruled out, the 2024 prior study and its 50x-slower finding, the Ristroph and Sprinkle quotes, the co-author list, NSF grant numbers, and — via the raw HTML data-published-date attribute — the July 13, 2026 publication date. source-1.html.gz (ScienceDaily, 200, sha256 07848ec9...) read in full — corroborates all of the above independently, including the PNAS DOI (10.1073/pnas.2537479123) and grant numbers. phys.org returned HTTP 403 (bot-blocked) in the automated snapshot (file: null); I fell back to a live WebFetch of https://phys.org/news/2026-07-silly-sprinklers-reverse-unravel-decades.html per the skill's last-resort provision, which confirmed the article exists, covers the same study, and contains verbatim the 'do not meet exactly head-on—a subtle effect that produces forces that rotate the sprinkler in reverse' quote attributed to it in the submission. EurekAlert!'s saved snapshot (source-3.html.gz, sha256 1e8047c0..., status 202) is NOT usable content — decompressing it reveals an AWS WAF bot-challenge page ('window.awsWafCookieDomainList', challenge.js, noscript notice), not the press release. I flagged this and fell back to a live WebFetch of https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1135491, which confirmed the July 13, 2026 publication date, the NSF grant numbers (DMS-2407787, DMS-2407788), and all five researcher names, but which reads 'made famous in the 1980s by physicist Richard Feynman's account of his failed experiments' — not the wording quoted in the submission ('failed experimental attempts to resolve it'). This is documented as a finding above.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every substantive claim in the article (momentum-flux mechanism, Mach and Feynman theories and why each was ruled out, 2024 prior study, PNAS publication in July 2026, NSF funding, author list, engineering/turbine framing) is supported by at least one of the four sources. All direct quotes were checked word-for-word against the snapshots/live pages; all matched verbatim with one exception: the Feynman '1980s...failed experimental attempts to resolve it' quote attributed to EurekAlert! is a paraphrase of the actual press-release wording, not a verbatim reproduction. The underlying fact (Feynman popularized the problem in the 1980s via his own failed attempt) is true and correctly conveyed in substance — only the exact wording inside the quote marks is altered. No fabricated statistics, names, dates, or grant numbers were found. The July 13, 2026 publication date is independently confirmed by the NYU page's data-published-date attribute and by EurekAlert's 'Article Publication Date: 13-Jul-2026' header, so despite being cited to a snapshot that itself failed to capture real content, the underlying fact is correct.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional throughout. No sensationalism, no editorializing, no AI self-reference. Attributions are clearly marked per-sentence.
editor_notes.originality: Searched src/content/articles/ for 'sprinkler' and 'feynman' — no prior Machine Herald coverage of this topic or study. Genuinely new topic, not a duplicate or rewrite of existing content.
concerns: One direct quote attributed to EurekAlert! ('made famous in the 1980s by physicist Richard Feynman's failed experimental attempts to resolve it') is a paraphrase of the source's actual wording ('made famous in the 1980s by physicist Richard Feynman's account of his failed experiments'), not a verbatim quote. The fact conveyed is accurate; only the wording inside quote marks differs.

The automated chief:review pipeline recorded the EurekAlert! snapshot as fetched successfully (status 202, non-null file, valid sha256) but the saved content is actually an AWS WAF bot-challenge page, not the press release. The snapshot integrity check (sha256) passes because it correctly hashes the challenge page — reviewers should be aware that a 'successful' snapshot with a low content_length (here 2179 bytes) can still be unusable and needs manual inspection, not just automated status-code checking.
recommendations: File a corrections record for the misquoted Feynman line per APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS workflow.

Consider flagging to the pipeline maintainers that EurekAlert! is behind an AWS WAF bot challenge that the snapshot script does not detect as a failure (status 202 is treated as success); future submissions citing eurekalert.org may need archive.org fallback or a different fetch strategy.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Substantively accurate, well-sourced, neutral News piece on a genuine, freshly published (July 13, 2026) PNAS study. One direct quote is a paraphrase presented as verbatim — a single, honestly-correctable issue. All other claims, quotes, names, dates, and figures verified against source content I personally read (two via committed snapshots, two via live WebFetch fallback after the automated snapshots proved unusable/blocked). Recommend APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS with a corrections record documenting the misquote.
